entries.title: ‘I am scared’: Careless People author Sarah Wynn-Williams on living under a gag order - and why it’s time to speak out against big tech
entries.summary: Since writing her bestselling exposé, the former employee has been forbidden from speaking publicly about Meta. In an exclusive extract from her Orwell lecture, she talks about corporate lawfare, and the growing backlash against NDAs George Orwell understood that what is missing often tells you more than what is there. In Nineteen Eighty-Four, there is a slot in the wall covered by a wire grate. T
entries.content:
George Orwell understood that what is missing often tells you more than what is there. In Nineteen Eighty-Four, there is a slot in the wall covered by a wire grate. They call it the memory hole. When a document becomes inconvenient to the authorities – a photograph that contradicts the official line, a newspaper that remembers the wrong promise, a name that is no longer supposed to exist – you simply feed it into the slot, whereupon it is whirled away on a current of warm air to enormous hidden furnaces where it burns.

The Party doesn’t argue with the past. It removes it. Controlling the past is one of its central tools of power: “Who controls the past controls the future: who controls the present controls the past.”

Control what people are allowed to remember or what they are allowed to know, and you control what they are able to imagine. Control what they can imagine, and you have already chosen their future for them.

Knowledge matters. People need to know what actually happened. But in 2026 the language of tech has taken on a quality of manifest destiny: the men in charge have determined how it should be, as though there could be no other way, even though none of us voted for any of it.

Control of the prevailing narrative is held tacitly: the only time this authority is given voice is when it acts, decisively, to silence an alternative account. Control over narrative is becoming the real power battle in technology. The aim is not to win the argument. The aim is to leave nothing to argue with. An absence. No record. No receipt. No contestable standard of truth. No common ground of fact against which anyone could measure those in power and expose their failures. Without memory or evidence, dissent has nothing to stand on. That is why memory matters. Why evidence matters. Why books matter.

You don’t need a Ministry of Truth to make a memory hole. An employment contract will do. An NDA will do. A court order will do. A legal bill – large enough, frightening enough, open-ended enough – will do very nicely. The modern memory hole does not smell of smoke. It smells of printer toner, fresh paper and billable hours.

In libel, truth is a defence. Under an NDA, truth is the offence.

The agreement is signed at the moment of maximum vulnerability, still reeling from an “incident” while the mortgage looms and the cardboard box of family photos sits in the front seat of the car. It is signed by the gig worker, the intern, the content moderator, the production assistant, the junior publicist, the stylist. There really is no better way to knock the whistle from someone’s lips. In a justice system based broadly on the principle that sunlight is the best disinfectant, NDAs grip the elbow of truth and stay it. This is a private form of censorship, enforced by private arbitration and the public courts.

Anyone targeted by an institution with a formidable legal department is, by definition, very vulnerable. It is one person against a building full of lawyers who seek only to protect the interests of the company, truth be damned. Some businesses are more powerful than states.

They have mastered corporate lawfare, letting slip the dogs of law on individuals who don’t have millions of pounds to defend themselves against these attacks brought on by trying to defy the memory hole. The word “brave” gets bandied around if you speak out despite all this. But “brave” should be for haircuts, not for telling the truth.

You do not have to silence everyone. You could never afford to. You only have to silence one person loudly enough that everyone else does the maths for themselves. These contracts seek to mute the truth, and they carry a big stick. The result is a society that has censored itself far more thoroughly than any Ministry of Truth ever could. No furnace required. Just fear, doing its patient and persistent work in the dark.

Recently, in the realm of entertainment, some big names have faced accountability or at least the prospect of it, because of women speaking out. Russell Brand was convicted, and David Walliams faces allegations. (Walliams has denied any wrongdoing in response to the allegations that he preyed on young women for sex.) In both cases, there are reports of NDAs being deployed to silence women. To ensure information that was clearly in the public interest was suppressed.

And while we should celebrate the courage and fortitude of the women who spoke out at unimaginable cost, and the media organisations, including the Guardian, whose investigations were instrumental in ensuring this information became public, I can’t help but notice that this accountability occurred at a time when the professional standing of these figures was already significantly diminished.

For a long time now it has felt as if certain sectors of society, including technology companies, act with impunity. I worry about all the powerful people who continue to benefit from silence and deprive us, the public, of information that can lead to warnings and ideally accountability. I worry we will only be allowed the truth about these companies when it no longer matters.

Whoever you are, whatever you believe, with an ever-more powerful elite there will come a day when you need to say something the powerful would rather you didn’t. And on that day, you will want three things: a place to say it that they do not own, a law that will not let them constrict you in grinding legal processes before bankrupting you for saying it, and people who will remember that you said it. The protections you are willing to fight for are the only ones that will be there when you need them.

Silencing the person who speaks is only half the job. The other half is making sure no one is paying attention. There is a detail in Nineteen Eighty-Four I used to skim past. Julia works in the Fiction Department of the Ministry of Truth. She services the novel-writing machines. These mass-produce literature as a commodity without any human creativity or critical thought. They use the same six stories, recombined endlessly to churn out formulaic slop for the proles.

The purpose of the novel-writing machines is to keep the proles distracted, passive and incurious. And it works. The proles never notice. The fiction machine has much in common with the feed: an endless scroll engineered by the brightest minds of a generation to keep your attention indefinitely. Nineteen Eighty-Four also gave us the Two Minutes Hate. A daily ritual of collective rage aimed at an enemy of the state. We have improved on it. Ours is continuous. Personalised. Delivered by push notification. And now with AI we have, literally, machines that write and humans that service them.

Orwell imagined the novel-writing machine as satire. We have built it. It was trained on the work of writers who were never asked. And sold back to them on a subscription. The Fiction Department of Nineteen Eighty-Four is now an industry. And it is the fastest growing one on earth. The memory hole removes what is true, and the fiction machine fills the space.

So much for what the machines do. The harder question is who owns them, and Orwell had a view on that too, though he was writing about a different technology. In October 1945, weeks after the atomic bomb was dropped, Orwell wrote a short essay exploring the deep connection between weapons technology and political power, observing that the shape of power in any age follows the shape of its decisive weapon. When weapons are cheap and simple – like the rifle – it empowers democracy and and gives “claws to the weak”, meaning ordinary people who can get hold of it have a fighting chance. When it is expensive and complex, like nuclear weapons, it concentrates power in the hands of a few and gives rise to oligarchic empires. And Orwell warned that these oligarchs might use the fear of the bomb to keep their populations suppressed, afraid to revolt.

Now think about the decisive technology of our own age. One that offers tremendous promise but also tremendous peril. The most advanced artificial intelligence takes investment measured in tens of billions. Chips made by a tiny number of firms, in a tiny number of places. Nobody builds this in a shed. Most governments do not have the resources to build it. A handful of companies can, mostly in just two countries.

Facing this, the most powerful technology in the world concentrated in a few hands, what would Orwell observe? Would he notice the democratic deficit around the technology? Would he worry about who can warn us today? Parliaments, the press, the law. They’re all outside the building. The people who know are on the inside. The researchers, the engineers, the ones who will say “I was there. I know what I saw. I will warn.” They’re the ones we need to protect from the memory hole. But in order to get inside the building in the first place, they needed to sign away their rights to speak.

Two years ago, current and former employees of the leading AI companies including OpenAI and Google DeepMind published an open letter asking for a right to warn. They asked for a prohibition on non-disparagement clauses and restrictive confidentiality clauses, anonymous reporting channels and no retaliation against employees. The letter said that the employees feared various forms of retaliation, given the history of cases across the industry. The fear was so pronounced some signed the letter anonymously.

The technology industry has learned to buy silence by contract, the courts enforce the sale, and we are relying on the silenced to warn us about its most dangerous product. That is the memory hole, installed in the place we can least afford it.

I have spent the most recent chapter of my career on what happens when this technology meets the weapons Orwell warned us about. Because it is happening. Artificial intelligence is rapidly being integrated into weapons, including command and control for nuclear weapons. Concentrated power all around.

Anyone who has worked closely with new technology will tell you the same thing. It is buggy. It does things you don’t expect and don’t understand. Now connect this technology to nuclear command and control. The question we need to ask: if someone on the inside saw something going wrong, would they be free to say so? Would they be free to warn?

We have spent the last two decades reacting. Responding to each harm long after it arrives. Arguing about what to ban, but never about what to build. That is not a vision. It is damage control. We have not yet tried, in any meaningful way, to create a vision for technology that serves our society. That delivers growth and opportunity. That chooses to mitigate harm as it builds a society with massive advances in health, in education, in science, and in the dignity of ordinary work.

We are living in an era that will be defined by technology. By removing what we can know, by creating a memory hole, the technology companies have controlled our knowledge, our common ground of facts and what we can imagine. But it doesn’t have to be this way. We can choose a different future. One that builds on the positive, the ineffable possibility technology offers while meaningfully grappling with its harm. But you cannot choose a different future if you are not allowed to describe the present one. Choosing requires knowing. And knowing requires that people are free to speak.

It is hard to explain what it is like to try to live under a gag order. Orwell gave us the thoughtcrime: you don’t have to act against the Party to be guilty. You just have to think the wrong thing. That’s what it feels like. To worry you might think the wrong thing and it could slip out. You start to rehearse sentences before you say them. You worry which word will produce the next legal letter. You begin, without ever meaning to, to censor yourself. So many times I go to say something and just … stop.

But even silence is no protection.

I want to acknowledge, here, that I am scared. If I am ultimately crushed and bankrupted, everyone will agree that it’s terrible, that NDAs are bad, that someone should have given her a voice, that someone should have supported her. And then they will forget. And the powerful will continue as normal.

But the thing about a memory hole: it only works if nobody outside it remembers what went in.

You are outside. You see. Please remember.

The silence is mine. It does not have to be yours.

entries.title: Children’s and teens roundup – the best new picture books and novels
entries.summary: A countdown to Christmas; musical mice; archeological treasure; a disgraced magician; a terrifying curse and moreAnd a Partridge in a Pear Tree by Fay Evans, illustrated by Jono Ganz, Flying Eye, £8.99 Partridge’s solitary splendour is rudely and cumulatively interrupted in this riotous, collage picture-book version of the well-loved carol – with a humorous twist at the end.Lost and Found at the G
entries.content:
And a Partridge in a Pear Tree by Fay Evans, illustrated by Jono Ganz, Flying Eye, £8.99

Partridge’s solitary splendour is rudely and cumulatively interrupted in this riotous, collage picture-book version of the well-loved carol – with a humorous twist at the end.

Lost and Found at the Gurdwara by Baljinder Kaur, Farshore, £7.99

Darshan is getting ready for the Nagar Kirtan procession with her grandparents, Bibi and Baba – but things keep going missing. This resplendent search-and-find picture book is a gorgeously detailed and evocative guide to traditional Sikh celebrations.

It’s Christmas Time by Birgitta Sif, Magic Cat, £16.99

Full of softly luminous illustrations, this Christmas countdown anthology contains brief, tender stories for sharing with the very small, as well as activities, such as making gingerbear cookies, paper stars and snowflakes.

Me and My Feelings by Dr Punam Krishan, illustrated by Verónika Cháves Morales, DK, £14.99

Bright, useful and fascinating, this colourful lift-the-flap guide will help children of 4 or 5+ to name, understand and process their emotions.

The Great Mouse Orchestra by Ella Risbridger, illustrated by Alice Courtley, Bloomsbury, £16.99

Little Jeremy Larkin believes passionately in the magical Great Mouse Orchestra that plays on the longest night of the year, though his family tease him that it’s just a mousetale. Can he create the perfect conditions to hear the Orchestra’s music? This delightful riot of house-that-Jack-built story, sparkling illustrations, tempting recipes and thoughtful activities is sure to become a 5+ seasonal favourite.

The Christmas Book by Katherine Woodfine, illustrated by Lizzy Stewart, Faber, £10

After Tómas’s grandfather, teller of wonderful tales, is lost at sea, Tómas is determined to cheer his family with surprise Christmas presents. Though there are no toys to be found in the wartime shops, the bookshop is still open. This poignant, joyful little book, inspired by the Icelandic tradition of Jólabókaflóđ, or Christmas Eve book-giving, is filled with the insistent power of hope and the lingering magic of shared stories, heightened by Stewart’s enticing and charismatic illustrations. A beautiful gift for 6+.

The Archaeologist’s Discoveries by Raksha Dave, illustrated by Natalia Cardozo, Magic Cat, £16.99

A tactile treat for 7 or 8+ history buffs, this guide to 10 significant artefacts, including a Roman dog mosaic, Tutankhamun’s sandals and the gold belt buckle of Sutton Hoo, features rich contextual detail, enthralling illustration and a raised panel on each double page where the treasure’s textures can be touched.

The Nightlights Collection - A Trilogy of Tales by Lorena Alvarez, Flying Eye, £25

Convent schoolgirl Sandy, who takes refuge from strict teachers in her drawings and imagination, enters a museum inside a turtle’s shell, is turned into a seed, and discovers strange worlds of beauty and terror in this hardback graphic novel collection for 8+, combining Nightlights, Hicotea and a new story, Sune, in pages full of polychromatic wonder.

A Scrap of Moss and Magick by Helen Parry, DFB, £7.99

Thirza, a servant girl in the house of a disgraced magician, isn’t pleased when her master’s niece comes to live with them, challenging her place as his indulged favourite. When she and Miss Cecily become friends, however, she realises some frightening truths about the Master’s orders - and about her own magical nature. Gripping, original, gutsy and satisfying, this dark folkloric debut will please 9+ Frances Hardinge fans.

Goodnight Silver by Abi Elphinstone, illustrated by Olivia Lomenech Gill, S&S, £8.99

Confirmed pessimist Emmy is braced for disaster when she and her parents travel to the remote Mongolian mountains, and when she gets accidentally separated from her family, all her worst fears seem to have come true. Then she finds a tiny snow leopard cub, the prey of ruthless hunters, and meets Tuli, a young poet who believes in impossible things. Can Emmy and Tuli get Silver to safety in the magical land of Winterfell - and can Emmy learn to hope again, despite past loss? An exhilarating, fast-paced wintry 9+ adventure, full of wild courage and fierce endurance.

A Conspiracy of Charming Monsters by Holly Black, illustrated by Solene Songer, Hot Key, £16.99

From a murderous eldritch warrior exiled to the mortal world (and discovering the riches of Costco along the way), to a tiny sprite on a colossal mission and a girl searching for the lost memories of her faerie love, these six sumptuously illustrated stories of Elfhame, including two entirely new tales, will delight 14+ fans of The Cruel Prince.

For Ever More by Sue Lynn Tan, Hodderscape, £22

When intrepid Yining returns to Mist Island, a home she hardly remembers, her hopes of peace are swiftly at an end. Hiding deadly dragon magic within her, trapped between hostile kingdoms and delicate alliances, she must find a way to contend with a terrifying curse and Queen Chunlei’s nightmarish ambitions to achieve immortal power – all while torn between her own conflicting desires. Layered with Chinese folktale, intricate worldbuilding and flawed, fascinating characters, the second part of Tan’s Cinderella retelling, a conclusion to the bestselling Never Ever After, is a hugely absorbing YA fantasy that can also be read as a standalone.

Have Yourself A Messy Little Christmas by Anna Zoe Quirke, Little Tiger, £9.99

Theo hasn’t seen her sister Juliet in five years. This Christmas, she’s escaping her controlling parents and tiny town to reconnect with Juliet and embrace her bisexuality in glamorous Manchester: yes to kissing girls, making peace with her past, dyeing her hair blue and embracing new experiences. But what about Otis - also bisexual, gorgeous, and keen on Theo - but undeniably a boy? Full of zinging wit and nuanced self-discovery, this seasonal YA romance is a delectable Yuletide treat.

entries.title: The Metaphor Zoo by Jeremy Butterfield review – how animals influence our language
entries.summary: A lexicographer reveals the surprising origins of common zoological turns of phrase, from fat cats to fur babiesAnyone who has grown up in the country knows that cows come home. They do it at tea time, like clockwork, because an unmilked cow is an uncomfortable cow. So how did “till the cows come home” come to mean never? Stranger still, when the phrase first appears in a 1587 commentary on St Pau
entries.content:
Anyone who has grown up in the country knows that cows come home. They do it at tea time, like clockwork, because an unmilked cow is an uncomfortable cow. So how did “till the cows come home” come to mean never? Stranger still, when the phrase first appears in a 1587 commentary on St Paul’s epistle to the Galatians, there is only one cow. By the time playwrights Beaumont and Fletcher take it up a few decades later, their characters are kissing and drinking till the cow – still single – comes home. What began as a promise of endless pleasure has become a sigh of futility.

Jeremy Butterfield’s Metaphor Zoo is full of such linguistic metamorphoses. Butterfield is a lexicographer by trade, the man the OUP entrusted with revising Fowler’s Modern English Usage. His guiding text is Lakoff and Johnson’s Metaphors We Live By (1980), which argues that metaphors don’t just colour how we speak but structure our thinking. In this sprightly but well-grounded book (metaphor alert), Butterfield asks what mental patterns lie behind the hundreds of animal phrases in English. Then in Johnsonian fashion, he sets about tracing the original, dating each through the Oxford English Dictionary and watching as it goes walkabout.

The results are enthralling. We think of animal idioms as folk wisdom handed down from time immemorial, but many turn out to be Victorian or later. Curiosity is first recorded killing the cat in the Waterford Mirror in 1858. The bee arrived in the bonnet with Thomas De Quincey in 1845; before that, Scots spoke of a head full of bees. The novelist Dinah Craik had parents settling into an empty nest in 1886, 70 years before “empty nesters” was coined in America. “Bats in the belfry” dates only from about 1901. “Fit as a butcher’s dog”, which sounds as if it came from some medieval almanac, is first recorded in 1938.

Inside these sayings are lodged small pieces of social history. “Wildcat” began as a term for the reckless, under­capitalised banks of 1830s America, whose dubious notes ended up in the pay packets of Irish canal labourers; a century later it had attached itself to strikes. The Cat and Mouse Act of 1913 released hunger-striking suffragettes when they were near death and rearrested them once they recovered, taking its nickname from the way a moggy plays with its self-catered dinner. The contempt in “a dog’s life” or “to die like a dog” makes more sense once you learn that in 1754 visitors to the Tower of London’s menagerie could avoid the thruppence entrance fee by bringing a dog or cat to feed the lions. Today people call their pets “fur babies” (abominable but still, technically, a metaphor).

Other phrases are genuinely ancient. The dog returning to its vomit runs from Proverbs through the Vulgate to Wycliffe and Chaucer. The ostrich burying its head descends from Pliny the Elder, who had it hiding in a bush. The image may originally come from a misreading of birds checking the temperature of eggs buried in sand. Some metaphors are so old they have gone underground altogether: “gregarious” comes from the Latin for a flock, and “pedigree” from the crane’s foot that archivists once drew to mark the relationship of one manuscript to another.

Butterfield’s best evidence that these phrases run deeper than English idiom comes from abroad. Where an Australian has kangaroos in the top paddock, a French person has a spider on the ceiling and a Dane has rats in the attic. English rains cats and dogs; German rains puppies; Danish rains cobblers’ apprentices and Welsh, gloriously, rains old women and sticks. The metaphors are still alive, too, as their routine mishearings attest. It is not unusual for people to talk about a “doggy-dog world”, chickens coming home to “roast”, or “one fowl swoop”. I was gratified to find that Butterfield suspects pug-ugly is a corruption of plug-ugly, the phrase I grew up with and still use, albeit with a quiver of doubt.

The slight trouble with the book is its tone. Butterfield is a serious scholar yet seems keen that we shouldn’t notice. So we get Beaumont and Fletcher as “the Jacobean stage’s Ant and Dec”, a “sheepiphany” on a Devon lane, and asides along the lines of “thank you, Microsoft!”. The jauntiness is not silly exactly, but it can feel like being talked down to by someone who needn’t do so.

Butterfield’s range, though, is wholly impressive. He moves from Shakespeare and Johnson to Strictly Come Dancing. It was TS Eliot, it turns out, who gave the OED its first recorded “bullshit”, in a poem of about 1910 that he hoped Wyndham Lewis would print in Blast. Butterfield also relishes Stormin’ Norman Schwarzkopf’s “bovine scatology” – a polite gloss the general did much to popularise.

This is a book to dip into rather than plough straight through (metaphors again). But it is a welcome addition to a crowded shelf of well-informed books on the English language, the sort that often find their way into the downstairs loo. It will equip every dinner party pedant and pub-quizzer with enough material to last till the cows, or rather the cow, comes home.

entries.title: Honey by Elizabeth Jenkins review – a rediscovered 60s classic of sex, money and power
entries.summary: The beautiful and mercenary Honey is a monstrously compelling character, in a novel with the ruthlessness of Richard Yates but more wit‘A sweet white grape of a book” is how Virginia Woolf described Elizabeth Jenkins’s first novel, Virginia Water, published in 1929 when Jenkins was 24. Jenkins may have detected a condescending note. She was wary of Woolf, having been invited into the Bloomsbury in
entries.content:
‘A sweet white grape of a book” is how Virginia Woolf described Elizabeth Jenkins’s first novel, Virginia Water, published in 1929 when Jenkins was 24. Jenkins may have detected a condescending note. She was wary of Woolf, having been invited into the Bloomsbury inner circle and then (in her own view, at least) just as quickly dropped again. Jenkins soon regretted the novel’s publication, apparently afraid acquaintances might recognise themselves, and tried to get rid of as many copies as she could.

Fortunately she wasn’t long deterred, either by her uneasy dealings with Woolf or her anxiety about Virginia Water; her subsequent literary career spanned 70 years, though most of her books had fallen out of print by the time she died in 2010. Perhaps this reissue of her 1968 novel, Honey, will bring Jenkins back into fashion. It ought to.

No one could accuse this book of grape-like sweetness. It follows beautiful and mercenary Honey Harper who, at 30, after a divorce and a string of affairs with wealthy men, marries Roland Ismay. Professionally successful and morally vacuous, Roly seems a suitable choice, but Honey is restless, concerned that her power over young men is waning. So naturally, when Roly’s ex-wife dies and his 16-year-old son Brian comes to live with them, Honey decides to seduce the boy.

Honey is a monstrously compelling character, and the early sections of the novel have the ruthless bleakness of Richard Yates, though funnier. Jenkins is witty on the sexual politics of the era, from the male teacher whose distrust of female wiles is so intense as to be “akin to the ancient fear of witchcraft”, to the female characters – Honey’s rivals and friends – who are forced to reckon with the limits of their own sexual power when exposed to the nuclear-blast force of Honey’s. The ever complacent Honey, meanwhile, will be left staggering from the shock of Brian’s indifference, and it is her increasingly desperate attempts to get his attention that drive the plot.

But more than sex, this is a book about money. One of the first things we learn about Honey is that “from the time she was 15 it was clear that she had not only beauty, but the kind of beauty that makes men ready to put down hard cash”. Her avaricious mother looks forward to Honey making a marriage that will entail a life of “mink coats and diamond watches”, and the mink coat in particular is a well-deployed motif. One of Honey’s first acts when Roly is sent the money for Brian’s upkeep is to persuade him to spend the bulk of it on a new mink coat for her, a mistake that will prove costly in both senses of the word. Jenkins is good on the ways in which, for Honey, money functions both as an end in itself and also as tangible evidence of her sexual power through the gifts she receives from men.

Since Honey is the novel’s strongest draw, its impact is diluted when she recedes to make way for a focus on Brian. He is a compelling character too in his way, with his combination of vulnerability and self-possession, and does add an emotional heft to the novel that Honey herself can’t provide. Jenkins is brilliant at balancing savagery with poignancy, as seen in The Tortoise and the Hare, one of her only books to have remained in print. But in this novel the two halves don’t quite fit, and I would have sacrificed any amount of emotional heft for more of Honey’s unhinged self-interest. We feel her absence most keenly in the second half, by which time we’ve spent a bit longer than necessary with the Cresswells, the kind but regrettably well-adjusted family of Brian’s best friend. When Jenkins is so good at dysfunction, do we really want her frittering away so many pages on healthy relationships?

The novel comes so close to perfection, to the pitiless, glittering beauty of the antiheroine herself, that I wanted a little more from it. Still, what we do get is a delight, a whole bunch of deliciously sour grapes. We should all be thrilled to see it back in print.

Honey by Elizabeth Jenkins is published by Daunt (£11.99). To support the Guardian buy a copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: Tonight the Music Seems So Loud by Sathnam Sanghera audiobook review – in praise of George Michael
entries.summary: The author blends teen memories and biographical details for a very personal tribute to the late singerWhen Sathnam Sanghera was a child, his older sisters fell under the spell of Wham!, the pop duo behind hits including Last Christmas and Young Guns (Go for It). Their brother soon caught the bug, becoming a diehard Wham! fan and following the career of singer George Michael into adulthood. In Ton
entries.content:
When Sathnam Sanghera was a child, his older sisters fell under the spell of Wham!, the pop duo behind hits including Last Christmas and Young Guns (Go for It). Their brother soon caught the bug, becoming a diehard Wham! fan and following the career of singer George Michael into adulthood. In Tonight the Music Seems So Loud, Sanghera blends memoir, biography and cultural criticism as he explores the life and work of Michael via themed chapters covering the singer’s sexuality, activism, addictions, his Greek Cypriot heritage and his songwriting prowess.

This is no objective trawl through the life of a distant pop star. Immersing himself in Michael’s world, Sanghera rides the same London bus route that he was on when he wrote Careless Whisper at 17 and visits the restaurant that once belonged to his father (Michael worked there briefly, until his dad fired him for mixing up the drinks orders).

Threaded through the narrative are vignettes from Sanghera’s life and his fandom, for which he was ridiculed frequently. When Michael was arrested for public lewdness in an LA public toilet in 1998, Sanghera was at university, where fellow students tacked the cover of a tabloid newspaper with the headline “Zip Me Up Before You Go-Go” on to his door.

The voice actor Homer Todiwala is the narrator who expertly navigates the book’s blend of the personal and biographical and captures the many contradictions of its subject. Michael was a private man who mocked his biggest tabloid scandals; a philanthropist who was quiet about his good works; and a teen pin-up who became one of the most celebrated artists of his generation.

Available via Picador, 10hr 24min

Further listening

A Court of Splintered Harmony

Sarah J Maas, Recorded Books, 12hr 1min

The sixth instalment of Maas’s all-conquering A Court of Thorns and Roses romantasy series finds an old enemy threatening the human lands. But will the Night Court be able to put aside its divisions and mount a defence? Narrated by Elizabeth Evans.

Firstborn Daughter

Katherine Ryan, Blink Publishing, 7hr 57min

The Canadian comedian examines “firstborn daughter syndrome”, or the quirks of eldest daughters that can lead them to organise and take charge, in this blend of memoir and social commentary. Ryan narrates alongside comics Joe Lycett, Aisling Bea and her eldest daughter, Violet.

entries.title: Patrick Radden Keefe’s London Falling named Waterstones book of the year
entries.summary: The word-of-mouth success of the journalist’s investigation into the death of a London teenager is ‘one of the defining features of the literary year’London Falling, Patrick Radden Keefe’s bestselling investigation into the mysterious death of a London teenager, has been named Waterstones book of the year.The book follows the parents of Zac Brettler, a 19-year-old who fell from the balcony of a lu
entries.content:
London Falling, Patrick Radden Keefe’s bestselling investigation into the mysterious death of a London teenager, has been named Waterstones book of the year.

The book follows the parents of Zac Brettler, a 19-year-old who fell from the balcony of a luxury London apartment after pretending to be the son of a wealthy Russian oligarch, as they discover the murky, dangerous underworld of the city that their son had been drawn into.

In a Guardian review, Ian Thomson called it “a scrupulously researched work of narrative nonfiction”. “Grimly absorbing from start to finish,” he wrote, the book “opens a window on to a world of financial dirty work and Walter Mitty-like fantasies of aspirational wealth.”

Waterstones’ head of books, Bea Carvalho, said its word-of-mouth success “has been one of the defining features of the literary year”. Reading nonfiction is “vital, enriching, gripping and the buzz surrounding London Falling has helped so many readers discover this,” she added.

Radden Keefe, a staff writer at the New Yorker whose previous book Empire of Pain won the Baillie Gifford prize, said that at heart London Falling “is a story about family – about parents and children, about the perils of contemporary adolescence, and about how little we sometimes know the very people we love most”. The book was shortlisted for this year’s Baillie Gifford prize.

Meanwhile, Taiwan Travelogue by Yáng Shuāng-zǐ, translated by Lin King, which won the International Booker prize earlier this year, was named fiction book of the year. Yáng said it was “especially precious to see this story about Taiwan embraced and adored by the booksellers at Waterstones”.

Is This a Plum? by Oscar-nominated director Dan Ojari and his eight-year-old son, Finn, was named children’s book of the year. The cut-out picture book began when the pair realised “a plum looks a lot like a hippo’s bum”, said Dan. “Me and my dad made this book together – it’s very easy to read and will probably make you laugh at least once,” added Finn.

The winners will receive the “full and committed backing of Waterstones shops and booksellers across the UK”, according to the company.

Also on the shortlist were Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke, Stations by Louise Kennedy, The Book of Birds by Robert Macfarlane and Jackie Morris, Redwood by Ben Macintyre, Land by Maggie O’Farrell, May We Feed the Kingby Rebecca Perry, Ottolenghi Simple Too by Yotam Ottolenghi and Verena Lochmuller, The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout and John of John by Douglas Stuart, among others.

Both the shortlisted titles and the book of the year are nominated and chosen by a panel of Waterstones booksellers.

Last year’s winner was The Artist by Lucy Steeds, while The Café at the Edge of the Woods by Mikey Please was named children’s book of the year.

  • London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe (Pan Macmillan, £22). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Have you read a book in recent weeks – fiction or non-fiction – that you’d recommend? Tell us all about it below.
